name: cv-baseline
hypothesis: Reference point: main's default config — linear probe on frozen YAMNet, Dropout(0.2), BinaryCrossentropy(label_smoothing=0.2), Adam 0.002 — under the general translation.
conclusion: The baseline every CV-era experiment compares against. Model kept at models/yamnet_medium_general.

name: binary-translation-cv
hypothesis: Collapsing every non-buzz label into one 'nonbuzz' class focuses the probe on the buzz boundary, instead of spending capacity on auxiliary classes.
conclusion: Neutral on the endpoint (-0.003), but binary's scores are far less portable across deployments: under one global threshold it looks much better (0.315 vs 0.262 pooled) because its score scale is consistent, not because it detects more. This pair is why the endpoint is per-deployment. Model kept at models/yamnet_medium_binary. Matches the pre-CV 'binary-translation' finding that multi-class auxiliary supervision is worth keeping.

name: context-stack
hypothesis: Buzz is sustained and the hard negatives are transient; stacking each frame's embedding with t-1 and t+1 gives the probe the duration cue it currently throws away.
conclusion: Positive, +0.050; 8/11 folds up, 6/8 among folds with >=3000 val frames. Cheapest structural win so far — no re-extraction. Not shippable until stack_context is mirrored in the inference wrapper (model.py feeds 1024-dim to a 3072-dim model). Eval is optimistic: snip frames all share a label so neighbours always agree, unlike continuous audio. Next: mirror in inference, sweep k=2,3, investigate the willard regression.

name: yamnet-combined
hypothesis: YAMNet's 521 AudioSet class scores are a nonlinear read of the same audio that a linear probe cannot construct for itself; concatenating them with the 1024-d embedding (1545-d) should add usable signal.
conclusion: Positive but modest, +0.016; 7/11 folds up, 6/8 among folds with >=3000 val frames and both declines there under 0.01. The two biggest movers (+0.180 at 2025-08-27/48, -0.153 at 2025-08-05/31) are both small folds and cancel; the latter early-stopped at epoch 6 and looks like a bad draw. Needed no code changes, but costs a re-extraction. The sigmoid scores are ~10x smaller than the embedding activations and nothing normalizes inputs - try standardizing the two blocks before judging the ceiling. Try before composing with context-stack.

name: context-embedder
hypothesis: exp/context-stack's +0.050 was measured on cached embeddings bucketed by label, so every frame's neighbours shared its own label - an artifact continuous audio can't reproduce, and the stacking lived in training code so the shipped model can't run it. Moving the same stack(t-1,t,t+1) into a new embedder, fed real neighbouring audio from the snip, should ship and measure honestly.
conclusion: Positive, +0.022; 7/11 folds up including the two largest movers (+0.140, +0.102), 4 down but only one (1_23, 315 val frames) is small enough to discount. Ships: model.py sizes its input layer from n_embeddings (3072) automatically and inference calls the same embed(). As predicted, well below context-stack's optimistic 0.256 - the gap is roughly the size of the same-label-neighbour artifact. willard (recorders/willard/2024-08-07/1_11) loses here too (-0.059), same fold context-stack lost on (-0.074), so that regression is a property of the deployment, not the cached-eval bug; worth the willard-regression listening pass next.

name: input-standardization
hypothesis: exp/yamnet-combined's +0.016 concatenated two feature blocks on very different scales (score block ~10x smaller than the embedding block) with nothing normalizing the input; a fixed Normalization layer, adapt()-ed on training folds only, should let the probe use the score block properly and shows whether the gain is a ceiling or an artifact of the scores being drowned out.
conclusion: Flat headline vs yamnet-combined (-0.004, 0.222->0.218; +0.012 vs cv-baseline), but carried entirely by one small/unreliable fold (2025-08-27/48, -0.156, 1570 val frames) that swung just as hard the other way when yamnet-combined was first measured. On the 8 folds with >=3000 val frames, standardization adds +0.014 on top of yamnet-combined (6/8 up) - the scale-mismatch hypothesis was real. Caveat: 10/11 folds ran the full 400-epoch cap under standardization vs a median ~120 for the unstandardized baseline, and best_val_loss came in higher despite sens improving in most folds - the fixed LR/patience were tuned for the old input scale and were never revisited. Not adopted on this evidence; see IDEAS.md's standardization-convergence for the LR/patience resweep this leaves open. No model shipped.

name: class-weight-fix
hypothesis: class_weight= passed to model.fit() is invalid for this model's multi-hot multi-label targets: Keras collapses y via argmax(y, axis=-1) to one scalar per sample, picked by class-index order (alphabetical), and applies it to the whole sample's loss rather than per-neuron. Any frame where ins_buzz co-occurs with an earlier-sorted class (ambient_*/animal/human) never gets ins_buzz's weight applied at all - verified against Keras 3.14.1 source and directly against the medium set (342/5478 pickles hit this). Replacing class_weight= with a custom loss (tf.nn.weighted_cross_entropy_with_logits, pos_weight per class) applies the same balanced weight table correctly per-neuron, reweighting only the positive term and leaving negative supervision untouched.
conclusion: Positive but modest, +0.013; 7/11 folds up. The two biggest movers each direction (+0.114 at 2025-08-12/1_114, +0.086 at 2025-08-05/31 up; -0.056 at JamesU, -0.038 at wooster down) are all folds with enough val frames (>3700) to trust individually, so this is a genuine majority-positive result, not a landslide masked by noise. The underlying bug is real and affected every CV-era log entry including cv-baseline itself (same weighting bug present in all of them), but the size of this correction is comparable to several logged wins rather than a wholesale invalidation - re-baselining the log is a judgment call for whoever reads this next, not decided here.

name: yamnet-native-buzz
hypothesis: YAMNet's own AudioSet-trained classification head might score insect buzzing better than our probe, since AudioSet is far larger than our field-recording set even if less task-specific. No training: take the frozen weight column + bias for AudioSet class 125 ('Buzz') off YAMNet's original Dense(521) layer and score it directly on our existing embeddings.
conclusion: Decisive negative. 9/11 folds scored, all near zero (0.000-0.034) including every large fold (4700-6900 val frames each) - not a small-fold artifact. Pooled ROC shows some separation (sens~0.30 at fpr~0.40) so the neuron isn't dead, just nowhere near usable at operating FPR. AudioSet's 'Buzz' class likely covers buzzers/electric buzz broadly rather than insect wingbeat specifically, and clip-level 521-way training doesn't sharpen a frame-level insect boundary. Only 'Buzz' tested, not 'Insect' or other AudioSet insect classes, but the gap is wide enough that off-the-shelf YAMNet classification is not worth pursuing further here.
